body: The Anchor at nine on a Saturday is the only lit window on the harbor side of Mission, a tank of yellow light with the sea lions hollering at it from the floats. Jack walks the last block from the corner with the duffel on his shoulder and his face put in order, and loses the order at the door, where the bell goes and the back booth turns around.

All four of them, and in the order he’d have bet. Laney is kneeling on the vinyl with a coffee spoon for a microphone. Margot sits upright against the window in a black turtleneck, Kevin beside her in a quarter-zip with his hands folded on the Formica, and in the corner, indoors, with the heat on, Theo, in the orange Browns hat and the brown-and-orange scarf Ma knitted in front of the news.
“Ladies and gentlemen,” Laney says into the spoon, “from Youngstown, Ohio: his platform is world peace and the Cleveland Browns, in that order, though he has been wrong before—”
“Sit,” Margot says. “She has been doing this since eight-thirty.”
“I *rehearsed*,” Laney says.
He sits on the outside, next to Theo, with the duffel between his feet. Propped against the sugar dispenser like a place card is an index card in purple Sharpie.

body.title: An index card, propped against the sugar
body.text: WELCOME BACK. 1. PIE. 2. NO QUESTIONS. 3. SEE ITEM 2.

body: “Item three refers the reader to item two,” Margot says. “Item two forbids the reader to ask why. The document is a closed loop.”
“It’s a *formatting choice*,” Laney says.

It is Laney being Laney: a welcome home with an agenda and a pie. Jack laughs, and keeps laughing a little past the joke, and Theo, who has not laughed, watches him do it with his chin in the scarf, as at a fever breaking.
Theo has already paid. A fifty sticks out from under the napkin dispenser, and nobody has ordered.
“You haven’t ordered,” Margot says.
“It’s called faith, Lindqvist,” Theo says. “Look it up.”
“I did. It isn’t that.”
“Theodore,” Laney tells the table, “has not taken that hat off since Christmas. He *slept* in it.”
“It’s a family heirloom,” Theo says.

He was in the middle of Youngstown when Jack came in, and he goes on with it: the eel, fried in rounds in a Pyrex at Frank’s elbow, which is a penance, for the men; Rosie, who has the Latin now, *Callinectes sapidus*, beautiful swimmer, savory, and says it at the table like a grace; Gina and the Flip camera; the stocking with his name on it in glitter glue, still wet on Christmas morning.
“Theodore cried at a stocking,” Laney says.
“Glitter is an irritant.”
He gets every detail right and tells it better than it happened, and Jack lets him have all of it and doesn’t add a word.
“Contestant Lindqvist,” Laney says, and points the spoon. “Portland.”
“Instructive.”
“That means awful.”

“It means my mother and her colleagues spent Christmas Eve arguing over whether Christmas is derivative of the Saturnalia, and I was asked to adjudicate. I said it was a category error. No one spoke to me until the pie.”
“Fourteen relatives, fourteen knees,” Kevin says, to nobody in particular. “My mother tells everyone I’m already a doctor, so they’ve started paying in rice cookers.”
“Mine was Dallas,” Laney says. “Mama cried at the fireworks *before* the fireworks. We have it on tape.”
Kevin has been studying Jack’s face with his head tilted. “Respectfully,” he says, “you look rested.”
“I was in Ohio.”
“I know. That’s the finding.”
“You’ve acquired a glow,” Margot says. “In Ohio. In January. That’s a statistical anomaly.”
“Lentils. Two spoons. I’m told I’ll be rich by Easter.”
“That is a folk belief in legume form,” Margot says.

Gloria arrives at the end of the booth with one plate, no pad, no check: a wedge of boysenberry with its insides running purple onto the china. She sets it in front of Jack and a fork beside it, says, “Tuesday. Seven,” and goes. Through the pass-through the kitchen radio is playing the song that has been on every radio in America since the fall, and Rudy, at the grill with his back to the booth, raises a spatula in Jack’s direction without turning around and says “Mijo,” softly, and not a decibel more.
Theo looks at the pie. Then at Jack. Then he takes a long drink of water.
“Since when,” Laney says, “do you eat boysenberry?”
“That was a question,” Margot says.
“That was an observation with a question mark on it.”
“Since Gloria put it in front of me,” Jack says, and picks up the fork.
“Okay. Business.” Laney taps the spoon on the card. “Tomorrow at four I’m getting Lena. Kevin’s driving. Her grandmother sent a king cake, and she is carrying it through two airports on her *lap*.”
“I know,” Jack says.
Laney looks at him over her Dr Pepper and takes her time with the straw. Then the spoon is a microphone again.
“So, fireman. Who picked you up?”
“Item two,” Margot says.
“It’s not a question. It’s a *logistics inquiry*.”
Theo studies a menu he has known by heart since August.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band.

response: “Shuttle,” Jack says.
“The seven fifty-eight SuperShuttle,” Theo says, before the word has finished. “He tipped the driver four dollars. I saw the receipt.”
Jack has given them a noun. Laney turns and looks at Theo for a long time, and Theo gives her back a face you could deposit.
Under the noise Kevin leans across the corner of the table. “My mother has a girl from our parish she wants me to call.”
“Of course she does.”

“Clare. She’s at Marisol. She plays the violin in the Mass band.” He is smiling when he says it, the Newman Center smile, and he keeps it exactly where it is until Margot asks what the two of them are whispering about.
“Pie,” Kevin says.
“Item one,” Laney says, and taps the card with the spoon, and the booth lifts four water glasses and a Dr Pepper to it.
“A Swede,” Jack says.
“That’s not an answer,” Margot says. “That’s a nationality.”
Theo puts his face in the scarf and leaves it there.
“And that,” Laney announces to the room, “is a *no comment*.”
Under the noise Kevin leans across the corner of the table. “My mother has a girl from our parish she wants me to call.”
“Of course she does.”

“Clare. She’s at Marisol. She plays the violin in the Mass band.” He is smiling when he says it, the Newman Center smile, and he keeps it exactly where it is until Margot asks what the two of them are whispering about.
“Pie,” Kevin says.
“Item one,” Laney says, and taps the card with the spoon, and the booth lifts four water glasses and a Dr Pepper to it.
Jack taps the card with the fork. “Pie first. Item one.”
Laney puts a hand to her chest. “He *read* it. I wrote that in Terminal E at DFW with a Sharpie I took off a child.”
“You did not take it off a child,” Kevin says.
“He wasn’t using it.” She turns to the booth, beaming. “I hate it when the rules work.”

“Of course she does.”

“Clare. She’s at Marisol. She plays the violin in the Mass band.” He is smiling when he says it, the Newman Center smile, and he keeps it exactly where it is until Margot asks what the two of them are whispering about.
“Pie,” Kevin says.
“Item one,” Laney says, and taps the card with the spoon, and the booth lifts four water glasses and a Dr Pepper to it.

body: Priya’s laminated sign is back on the fourth-floor stairwell door: WELCOME BACK. QUIET HOURS RESUME AT 10 P.M., SUNDAY–THURSDAY. THIS MEANS YOU. —P.R. From behind the door of 420 comes Doug’s voice, patient, to a stranger on a headset: “Dude. No. *Behind* it.” The strap of the duffel is cutting into Jack’s shoulder. He is still smiling a little, at nothing, in a hallway, and he lets the strap dig.

The door of 412 opens before he gets to it. Laney comes out with her laptop shut under one arm and her phone in the other fist, in the Pi Lam hoodie, no lipstick, her mouth a straight line. She sees him. For the first time since August she looks at him and says nothing, not *fireman*, not his name, and goes by with her shoulder a few inches from his duffel and down the hall to the east stairwell, and the fire door shuts on the sound of her feet.
“Laney?” he says, to the door.
Jack looks after her. Then he goes in.

412 has one lamp lit and the window open a crack, and the room smells of kelp and, faintly, of somebody’s vanilla. Theo is on his bed in his socks with his eyes on the ceiling and the orange hat hanging from the bedpost by its brim. The iPhone on his chest is face-up, and it buzzes and lights the underside of his chin. He looks at it, and turns it face-down.
“Hey,” Jack says.
“Congratulations, Costigan.” To the ceiling. No *Father Jack*, no *my moral compass*: just the surname, laid down flat.
“Thanks.” Jack lets the duffel off his shoulder onto his bed.
“Callender changed it herself,” Theo says.
It takes Jack a second. “How do you know?”
“Because Corinne would have made it a premiere.”
Theo turns his head on the pillow, looks at him, and looks back up. Jack sits down on his own bed with his shoes still on.
“Go to sleep,” Theo says. He reaches over his head and the lamp goes out. In the dark: “Monday is going to be a long day.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word.

s17.slug: MONDAY · 12:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR, THE STEPS
body: The twelve-ten on the first Monday back is thin and a little dazed, and Fr. Osei has the green on, the first green since November. The Gospel is Mark, the first chapter, the shore: *Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.* Simon and Andrew abandon their nets on the spot, and the next two are called while they are mending theirs. “Ordinary Time,” Osei says in a homily of ninety seconds, “is when He asks. Nothing is happening. This is why He picks it.”

At the sign of peace Becca, across the aisle, turns around and holds out her hand, and he takes it. “Peace be with you.” “And also with you.” Her hand is dry and brief, and she is facing the altar again before his has let go.

body.text: Jack goes up with the line and receives, and comes back down the side aisle with his hands folded and his eyes on the tile.
body.else: When the line forms Jack stays where he is, with his hands on the back of the pew in front of him, and makes a spiritual communion, the old prayer, to the sound of other people’s shoes.

body: Afterward the line out the door is a Monday line: Mrs. Fitch with the announcements and a lanyard, Joey Abruzzo telling a freshman, at the volume of a kickoff, that the twelve-ten is the best-kept secret on campus, and under the bell Osei, in the green, with his glasses on their cord, saying *Akwaaba, akwaaba* to everyone who has been away. When it is Jack’s turn Osei takes his hand in both of his own and holds him at arm’s length.
“Let me look at you.” It is a physician’s look and it lasts one second. “You have your color. In December I was prepared to prescribe sleep.”
“I slept.”
“So I see.” He lets go of the hand. “Well?”
“Father. The errand.”
“Ah. And?”
“Father Dom says we’ll see.”
The laugh starts somewhere near the belt and keeps climbing, and heads turn the length of the steps. “Then we will,” Osei says, and wipes an eye with the back of his wrist.

body.text: “I went at home, Father,” Jack says. “Saturday before last.”
“Three-thirty,” Osei says. “I’ll leave the light on.”
“Welcome back, Jack,” Osei says. And Jack doesn’t ask about Saturday.

body: At the bottom of the steps someone has been waiting her turn, and now she isn’t: Becca, with her grandmother’s rosary wound twice around her wrist and her braid over one shoulder and the clipboard against her chest, coming up toward him with her face already open. Jack is on the third step from the top. He stays on it. The strap of his bag is in his fist.

“I saw,” Becca says. She stops one step below him, so that their eyes are level. “Last night, on the News Feed. I made myself wait until after Mass to decide how I felt, because I didn’t want to decide it in the middle of the Creed. And I decided. She’s so pretty, Jack. And she looks — she looks really happy. I’m really happy for you.”

“I prayed for you over Christmas,” she says. “That you’d be happy. So.” She laughs at herself, short, and pushes the braid back. “I also did a Glory Be for both of you at breakfast. Twice. It’s short. And I’m good, by the way, in case you were going to wonder. I have a hermit crab and a lab section.”
“And Thomas saw snow,” she says. “In Coeur d’Alene. He did not care for it.” She taps the clipboard. “Coffee and Donuts is still Sundays. The maple bars are yours. I told Mrs. Fitch.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home.

choices.text: “Thank you, Becca. That means a lot.”
choices.key: The first day back, Becca found you on the steps of St. Brendan’s and told you she was happy for you. You thanked her.
response: “Thank you, Becca,” Jack says. “That means a lot.”
“Good,” Becca says. “It’s supposed to.”
She gives his sleeve two pats. When he looks down, the buckle of the strap has printed a line across his palm, and he opens the hand and shuts it again.

“Sunday,” she says. “Don’t make Mrs. Fitch do your order from memory.” She goes down the steps to the curb, where Eli’s red Ranger is waiting with its Idaho plates, and Jack watches the Ranger take two tries to start.

choices.key: The first day back, Becca found you on the steps of St. Brendan’s and told you she was happy for you. You told her you should have told her yourself.
response: “I should’ve told you myself,” Jack says.
“Why?” Becca frowns up at him, honestly trying to see it. “You don’t owe me that, Jack.”

She says it so kindly that the strap leaves a line across his palm. Then she sets the clipboard on the step, comes up the one step, and hugs him anyway, her cheek cold against his collar and the beads of the rosary hard against the back of his neck.

“Go,” she says into his shoulder. “You’ll be late for whatever it is. You always want to be early to the arguments.” She lets go, tucks the braid back, picks the clipboard up off the step, and goes down toward the curb and Eli’s Ranger.

choices.key: The first day back, Becca found you on the steps of St. Brendan’s and told you she was happy for you. You asked about the hermit crab.
response: “Thomas saw snow?” Jack says.

Her face changes, and out comes the entire Christmas of Thomas in the Tupperware. Thomas went through the X-ray at Santa Barbara, and the man said, “Ma’am, is that a crab?” and she said, “Hermit,” and the man said, “Of course it is.” He rode to Coeur d’Alene on a heating pad turned to low. The youngest carried him out onto the porch in a mitten, and Becca held him in her glove at nineteen degrees for ninety seconds, which is the limit, she looked it up, and he pulled all the way in and then walked straight to the heating pad and wouldn’t look at anyone.
“He’s back on the tank. Thursday. He’s still not speaking to me.”
Jack lets her tell all of it. Somewhere in the middle of the mitten he lets go of the strap.
“Anyway,” Becca says. “Sunday.” She squeezes his arm, and goes down the steps to Eli’s red Ranger and its Idaho plates.

choices.key: The first day back, Becca found you on the steps of St. Brendan’s and told you she was happy for you. You let her hug you and didn’t say anything.
response: Becca sets the clipboard on the step and hugs him, quick and hard, with the strap of his bag crushed between them, and he gets one arm around her.
“Okay,” she says into his shoulder. “I have bio.”

She lets go, picks the clipboard up off the step, and goes down to the curb, where Eli’s red Ranger is waiting with its Idaho plates. It starts on the second try. The strap of his bag has printed a line across his palm.
